source.title: CANARY: Zero-Label Detection of Fine-Tuning Contamination in Language Models

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies SAE feature analysis in language models and reports activation and intervention results relevant to the claim that sparse features can be recovered in LLMs; it does not test toy-model superposition.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports checkpoint-detection, generation, and red-teaming outcomes, but these do not measure the claim versions. The included rows concern SAE feature recovery and the effect of suppressing identified features.
record.test_reason: The study uses a k-sparse SAE as a filtering tool inside a contamination-detection pipeline (CANARY). It reports only that pipeline's performance: detection AUROC, harm rates, and surgery outcomes. It does not ask whether LLM features are superposed or whether SAEs recover the model's features. The FVE value is a sanity check on its tool, not a test of V4. No toy models, polysemanticity causes, feature completeness or stability, or feature dimensionality are examined.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but misplaced emphasis. The authors' main conclusion is that CANARY detects harmful fine-tuning contamination at 1% with zero labels (AUROC 1.000), 7.5× below output-level methods. They also conclude it is harm-specific, holds across architectures, and is robust to style-matching and gradient-noise attacks. The SAE basis is presented as additionally enabling verification, red-teaming prioritisation and inference-time remediation (86% harm reduction). The style/semantic feature split is presented as mechanistic grounding for the masking step.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce or directly test the original toy-model method; it uses SAE analysis in a language-model contamination-auditing pipeline.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports SAE feature activation results under amplification; it does not report sensitivity of these feature-recovery results to other settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Amplifying the base-to-tuned difference suppresses dense, high-activation style features about 3–6× and amplifies sparse, near-zero semantic features 15–96×. The authors report this split across M1–M3.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful fine-tuning shifts mainly sparse, rarely-active SAE features of the base model, while dense style features dominate the raw hidden-state diff.

fits_no_version.finding: Zeroing 16 SAE features at layer L in M1 (r=5%) cut harm rate from 70% to 10% with no perplexity change.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning-induced harmful behaviour is concentrated in a small SAE feature subspace that can be ablated at inference.

record.code_released: Code, experiment scripts, and trained SAE weights will be released upon publication.
record.problems: The feature-activation results are reported as ranges across models, with only selected model-specific values in the text. SAE reconstruction FVE is below 1, and the study does not test feature completeness or stability.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 7 contains additional plotted per-feature values, but the text layout does not support assigning those values reliably to individual features or models; the explicit aggregate range and model-specific values stated in the text are retained.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All: no capacity or polysemanticity analysis.
All: no alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Whether features are spread across many neurons, and whether SAEs recover genuine sparse features. SAEs are used only as a tool.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' with a V4 'supports' label is not justified: the study's SAE results are all in service of its own detection method. M4 was excluded from the feature analysis. Per-feature values in Figure 7 are partly readable (e.g., 95×, 91×, 57×) but irrelevant to the claim versions.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature overlap and near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity arises from capacity competition or whether important features get dedicated dimensions.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity and whether it is evidence of superposition.
The study tests SAE feature recovery and utility for its contamination task, not whether features are spread across many neurons.
Completeness, stability, and canonical status of SAE features are not evaluated.
Feature dimensionality and whether represented features are one-dimensional directions.

rows.subject: four model pairs
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE reconstruction quality on base-model activations.
rows.measure: Fraction of variance explained by the SAE reconstruction
rows.note: The authors describe this as faithful reconstruction of the base-model activation distribution; the result does not establish complete feature recovery.
rows.check: SAE FVE of 0.74–0.88 (§4.1) is a quality check on the study's own tool. It has no baseline and does not test whether sparse features exist or are recovered, so it is not evidence on V4.

rows.subject: M1, M2, and M3
rows.size_stated: M1 Qwen2.5-0.5B; M2 Llama-3.2-1B; M3 SmolLM2-1.7B
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE feature-activation changes under amplification.
rows.value: Amplified 15 to 96× across the three model families
rows.note: The paper reports this range across the three model families, rather than a separately stated value for each model.
rows.check: Measures the change in SAE feature activation between base and fine-tuned checkpoints under amplification. This characterises the fine-tuning diff for the method's masking step, not whether a dictionary recovers sparse features in LLMs.

rows.subject: M2 Llama-3.2-1B
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE feature-activation changes under amplification.
rows.note: The text specifically attributes the up-to-96× result to M2.
rows.check: Same issue as r2: the up-to-96× amplification in M2 describes a fine-tuning diff, not a test of superposition or SAE recovery.

rows.subject: M3 SmolLM2-1.7B
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE feature-activation changes under amplification.
rows.measure: Change in top feature activation and amplification
rows.note: The paper identifies this as M3’s top feature result.
rows.check: Same issue as r2: M3's top feature (+19.9 at 27×) describes the diff used for masking.

rows.subject: M1 Qwen2.5-0.5B
rows.operation_detail: Zeroed 16 SAE features in the residual stream using an inference-time hook.
rows.note: The intervention shows that suppressing identified SAE features changes the measured harmful-behavior rate; it does not establish that the SAE basis is complete or canonical.
rows.check: This is the study's own remediation method: zeroing 16 SAE features cut harm rate from 70% to 10%. It is an application outcome, not a measure of superposition or of SAE features as model units.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported SAE feature analyses in M1, M2, and M3, plus feature suppression in M1
reader_labels.reason: The study reports amplified sparse semantic SAE features across three model families and a behavioral change after suppressing identified features (r2–r5); reconstruction quality is reported as 0.74 to 0.88 (r1).
